implementation_notes: Kotlin has a dedicated construct for this pattern: an inline value class wraps a value to create a more domain-specific type without the allocation a normal wrapper costs, because the class is a subset of value-based classes (no identity, represented by the underlying value in generated code). Validation belongs in the init block, which runs on every construction, so the value class is its own smart constructor; a private constructor plus a companion parse keeps raw values out. Prefer it over a data class whenever the type is a single value and does not need inheritance or per-instance identity.
pitfalls: Boxing is silent: in collections, as map keys, in nullable positions (UserId?) and as generic arguments the wrapper is boxed, so the zero-allocation claim holds only for direct parameters, returns and fields.
Value classes have no identity and cannot extend classes: === compares underlying values, and interfaces (not base classes) are the only abstraction mechanism available.
Mangled JVM signatures (parse-impl) surface in Java interop, reflection and frameworks that expect a normal class.

variants.name: data class wrapper
variants.implementation_notes: Where the value must be nullable, used as a generic argument, needs identity or inheritance, or the Kotlin version predates 1.5, an ordinary data class still gives a distinct type with generated equals/hashCode/toString/copy and a validating init block. It allocates on the heap, which is irrelevant for identifiers and measurable in hot numeric loops - the reason the value class is the default and this is the fallback.
pitfalls: The generated copy() lets any caller rebuild the value while keeping the class, so an invariant that is not rechecked in init can be circumvented.
A data class is a reference type: == is structural but === distinguishes instances, and the extra object is visible in allocation-sensitive code.
